summary: Explains the difference between information models and data models for defining managed objects in network management. It analyzes how specifications from the IETF and bodies such as the ITU and DMTF fit into each category, to reduce ongoing confusion about the terms.

plainLanguage.summary: An information model describes managed objects and their relationships without choosing an implementation. A data model adds the protocol and implementation details needed to build or exchange that information.

questions: difference between information and data models
what is a data model in network management
subtitle: A distinction between conceptual information models and implementation-level data models.

tldr.problem: Network-management discussions used information model and data model in inconsistent ways.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how the models differ in purpose and abstraction, then classifies examples from several standards organizations.
tldr.outcome: One information model can lead to several data models, although the distinction has a gray area.

today: RFC 3444 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It explains terminology for distinguishing information models from data models.

sections.title: Why the Terms Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
Network management uses languages such as SMI, SPPI, and MOF to define managed objects. Discussions about these languages revealed that participants did not agree on what the terms Information Model (IM) and Data Model (DM) meant.

This RFC records the result of an NMRG workshop held to harmonize the terminology. It explains the reasoning and gives examples from the IETF and other organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: People were using two modeling terms in different ways. This RFC explains a shared distinction so discussions can be clearer.

sections.title: Two Models, Different Purposes
sections.content:
An information model describes managed objects at a conceptual level. It should hide details of a particular implementation or transport protocol and can describe relationships between objects.

A data model is more detailed and aimed at implementors. It includes protocol-specific constructs. Several data models can be derived from one information model because the same concepts can be implemented in different ways.

The boundary is not always sharp. Some models include details that make it difficult to classify them as purely conceptual or purely implementation-specific.
sections.plainLanguage: An information model describes what the managed things are and how they relate. A data model explains how a particular system represents them.

sections.title: Information Models in Practice
sections.content:
Information models help designers describe a managed environment, operators understand it, and implementors see what their data models must represent. They may be written informally in natural language or presented in structured forms such as UML class diagrams.

The RFC notes that explicit information models are uncommon in IETF documents. Some MIB specifications include an informal description of the model behind them, but the RFC says many such descriptions are rudimentary or incomplete.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers can explain an information model in prose or diagrams. It gives implementors a guide without prescribing every encoding detail.

sections.title: Data Models and Examples
sections.content:
Data models define managed objects at a lower level of abstraction and explain how to map them onto protocol constructs. The RFC's examples include IETF MIB modules in SMI, PIB modules in SPPI, OSI MIB modules in GDMO, and DMTF CIM schemas in MOF.

These models differ in how they express details and relationships. For example, IETF MIB modules include object identifiers, indexing rules, access clauses, status, and conformance statements. The RFC classifies SMIng as a data model even though it is more protocol-neutral than some other IETF approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Data models contain the details a particular management protocol needs. The RFC uses MIBs, PIBs, and CIM schemas to show how different groups do this.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the meaning of the terms Information Model and Data Model has no direct security impact on the Internet. It defines terminology and does not specify a protocol.

The document's contribution is to clarify how the terms are used when describing network-management models.
sections.plainLanguage: These definitions do not change how Internet systems work. They clarify language used to describe management models.
